hero.title: Help your child feel understood, not defined by a difficulty.
hero.summary: Explore a thoughtful starting point for your child: their experience, the family context, and a care plan that fits their age and everyday life.

panel.title: Understand the care before choosing a time.
paragraphs: Read about the work, compare clinicians, and choose the starting appointment that fits. A request is not a confirmed booking.

items.title: How the first conversations work
items.text: Start with the process, not a list of labels.

items.title: Your questions, answered
items.text: Format, participation, and practical next steps.

sections.title: Begin with the child, not a behavior label.
paragraphs: An evaluation considers a child's experiences in context rather than turning one difficult afternoon into a diagnosis. NIMH describes gathering developmental and family information, observations, and relevant information from school as parts of understanding what support may help.

For your inquiry, a concrete description is useful: what you noticed, when it began, where it happens, what is different from before, and what your child says about it. Include strengths and interests as well as difficulties. Those details help make the first conversation about a whole person.

Child therapy is not a promise that an adult can hand over a behavior to be fixed. The practical goal is a clearer understanding of the concern and a plan that the child and caregivers can participate in. The service, caregiver role, and clinician's actual age range need to fit.

panel.title: Your child is more than the hardest moment.
paragraphs: There can be room for worry, grief, frustration, changes at home, and the things your child enjoys. An introductory inquiry does not require you to know the explanation.
Ask about the clinician's age range before choosing a time. A broad child-service page does not mean every clinician works with every age.

sections.title: Different observations lead to different questions.

items.title: Worry and avoidance
items.teaser: What feels difficult to begin, join, or return to?
paragraphs: A child may describe a particular fear clearly, or you may first notice reluctance around a routine. Compare what is happening in different settings without deciding that one person's account cancels another's. A fictional example is a child who manages school but needs a long transition when returning home.
Bring the pattern to a clinician rather than designing a confrontation with the fear on your own.

items.title: Big emotions and difficult transitions
items.teaser: What happens before, during, and after the moment?
paragraphs: Instead of only saying that a child melts down, describe an ordinary sequence: the activity that ended, a request that followed, the response, and how the child settled afterward. That offers a starting point for questions about expectations, support, and context.
The observation is not proof of a diagnosis, parenting failure, or deliberate misbehavior. It is information to understand.

items.title: Loss or a change in family life
items.teaser: What does the child understand, and what are they still asking?
paragraphs: A move, loss, or change at home can raise practical questions as well as feelings. You might notice repeated questions, a change in play or routine, or uncertainty about what stays the same. Start with what your child has actually expressed.
Care should leave space for the child's words rather than asking them to adopt an adult's complete account.

items.title: Share the context
paragraphs: Before the appointment, ask what the clinician wants from caregivers and how the child will be introduced to the process. Bring a brief timeline and practical concerns through the approved intake route. Do not send private records through a marketing link.

items.title: Explain the plan at the child's level
paragraphs: The clinician can explain what a session is for, how participation works, and the relevant privacy boundaries. Ask whether the first visit involves caregivers, the child, or both. The answer depends on the actual service rather than a rule supplied by this page.

items.title: Notice changes in ordinary life
paragraphs: Discuss what a useful change would look like at home or school, how it will be reviewed, and whether any between-session activity is appropriate. The work should not be judged solely by whether a child appears calm in the office.

sections.title: Different people can have different parts in care.

items.title: The child's space
paragraphs: A child needs an explanation of what they are being invited to do. They may have a different priority from the adult who arranged the visit. Ask how their perspective will be heard, including when they are quiet or disagree.

items.title: Caregiver participation
paragraphs: NIMH describes caregiver involvement and monitoring progress as common parts of child treatment. The specific arrangement is individualized. Clarify what updates caregivers receive, how concerns are shared, and which home or school conversations need permission.

sections.title: Replace a broad complaint with a question you can examine.

items.title: The first description
paragraphs: A fictional caregiver says every school morning is a battle.

items.title: The closer look
paragraphs: The difficulty appears during the transition from breakfast to leaving, but not on all mornings. The child has their own explanation of what feels hard.

items.title: The starting point
paragraphs: The first discussion can clarify the sequence and what further information is needed before deciding on a care plan.

reveal.title: Look beneath the first explanation
paragraphs: This is an observation example, not a prescribed parenting strategy. Different explanations may require different kinds of support.

sections.title: Find a clinician whose work fits your next step.
sections.intro: These profiles describe working with children. Read the biography and confirm the current service, age range, and availability.

sections.title: Answers before you begin.

items.question: Does my child need a diagnosis before we contact you?
paragraphs: You can inquire by describing your concern and asking about an evaluation or starting appointment. The website does not diagnose. A clinician can explain what assessment is appropriate and any requirements for the particular service.

items.question: Will sessions involve play?
paragraphs: Some child approaches use play, activities, or creative materials, but this page does not promise a particular method. Ask what your clinician actually offers for your child's age. The [play therapy guide](/play-therapy/) explains an approach; a guide existing is not confirmation that every clinician provides it.

items.question: Will I attend every session?
paragraphs: Do not assume so. Ask how the clinician proposes to involve you, which parts may be individual, and what information can be shared. The arrangement depends on the child, service, consent, and applicable requirements; it should be explained before you rely on it.

items.question: How can I explain the appointment to my child?
paragraphs: Ask the clinician for age-appropriate guidance. A neutral introduction could be that you are meeting someone to understand a hard part of life and look for helpful ways forward. Avoid describing therapy as punishment or promising that the clinician will take someone's side. This is a preparation example, not a required script.

items.question: Can the therapist work with the school?
paragraphs: Ask whether that coordination is part of the service and what consent or releases would be needed. A teacher's observation can be useful information, but school communication and record sharing are not automatic consequences of booking a visit.

items.question: When should we seek urgent help rather than wait?
paragraphs: If behavior is unsafe or a child talks about harming themselves or others, seek immediate help rather than an ordinary website appointment. For a mental health crisis in the U.S., call or text 988. For a life-threatening emergency, call 911.

sections.contact: For practical questions, [email support@mft.care](mailto:support@mft.care?subject=Service%20question). Please leave private clinical details out of the initial email.
